period: Old Kingdom, late 4th to early 5th Dynasty, c. 2500 BC
summary: A wooden priest so lifelike that the men who dug him up named him after their village headman. The nickname has stuck for over 160 years.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A standing man carved in sycamore wood, about 1.12 m tall, striding forward with a staff. Round face, double chin, a comfortable belly over a long kilt. The eyes are rock crystal set in copper, and they seem to follow you.
story:
In 1860 workmen digging for Auguste Mariette opened a mastaba at Saqqara, just north of Djoser's Step Pyramid. When this statue came out of the sand and stood upright, they cried out that it was their 'sheikh el-balad', the headman of their village. The name stuck, and guides still use it.

His real name was Ka-aper. He was a lector priest, who read the sacred texts aloud at rituals, and an army scribe of the king, a title that may link him with campaigns in the southern Levant. He lived around 2500 BC, as the 4th Dynasty gave way to the 5th.

The sculptor built him from at least six pieces of sycamore. Wooden statues were usually finished with a coat of plaster and paint, now mostly gone, so the grain shows. What remains is one of the most honest portraits in Egyptian art: not a god-like ideal but a well-fed, middle-aged official. A wooden statue of a woman from the same tomb is usually thought to be his wife.
details: The eyes: rock crystal with small copper plates. Step to one side and they still seem to watch you.
The belly and double chin: an official who ate well, and wanted to be remembered that way.
Joins in the wood at the shoulders and arms: he was built from several pieces of sycamore.
His left foot steps forward: the standard pose for a living man on the move.
fun_fact: Sheikh el-Balad is Arabic for 'village headman'. Ka-aper has been Egypt's most famous mayor for over 160 years without winning a single vote.
narration: If you have found him, this wooden man is Ka-aper, and he has one of the best nicknames in Egypt. In 1860 workmen digging for Auguste Mariette at Saqqara, just north of the Step Pyramid, pulled him out of a tomb and stood him up. They took one look and cried out: it is our sheikh el-balad, the headman of our village. The name stuck. His real titles were grander. Ka-aper was a lector priest, who read the sacred texts aloud at rituals, and a scribe of the king's army, around 2500 BC. He is carved from sycamore wood, in several pieces joined together, and he probably once wore a coat of plaster and paint, now mostly gone. What is left is an honest portrait: a round face, a double chin, a comfortable belly over his kilt. This is not a god-like ideal. It is a successful middle-aged official who ate well and wanted to be remembered that way. Now look at the eyes. They are rock crystal set in copper, and from a step to one side they still seem to follow you.

summary: A dwarf who rose to high office sits beside his wife, and the sculptor used the children to make the family look perfectly balanced.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A small painted limestone group, only about 22 cm high. Seneb sits cross-legged on a block, his wife Senetites beside him with her arm around him. In front, exactly where a seated man's legs would hang, stand their son and daughter, fingers to their lips.
story:
Seneb lived around 2520 BC and was buried in tomb G 1036 in the Western Cemetery at Giza, among the officials of the pyramid age. Hermann Junker found the tomb in 1926. It had been robbed long ago and no trace of the bodies remained, but this group survived.

Seneb was a man of rank. His monuments list about twenty titles, among them overseer of dwarfs and overseer of weaving in the palace, and he took part in the funeral services of Khufu and Djedefre. His wife Senetites, of normal height, was a priestess of Hathor and Neith. Three children are named; only two are shown, probably for symmetry.

The sculptor faced a puzzle: how to show a short man beside a taller wife with dignity. The answer was to seat him cross-legged, like a scribe, with his head level with hers, and to fill the space below him with the children. Nothing here mocks him. Dwarfism was not treated as a defect in ancient Egypt: texts advised respect for people with disabilities, some dwarfs held prestigious posts, and two gods, Bes and Ptah, could take dwarf form.
details: The children where Seneb's legs would be: a boy and a girl, each with a finger to the mouth, the sign of a child.
Skin colours: Seneb red-brown, Senetites pale. The usual male and female convention.
Senetites' arm around her husband: a gesture of partnership found in many Old Kingdom couples.
The hieroglyphs on the base naming the family.
fun_fact: Among Seneb's twenty titles is 'overseer of dwarfs'. The man in charge of the palace dwarfs was one himself, and he put it on his tomb.
narration: If you have found it, this small painted family group is Seneb, his wife Senetites and two of their children, carved around 2520 BC. Seneb was a dwarf, and he was also a man of rank. His tomb at Giza, among the officials of the pyramid age, lists about twenty titles, among them overseer of weaving in the palace and overseer of dwarfs, and he took part in the funeral rites of King Khufu and King Djedefre. Senetites, of normal height, was a priestess of Hathor and Neith. Now look at how the sculptor solved his puzzle: how to show a short man beside a taller wife, with dignity. Seneb sits cross-legged, like a scribe, so his head is level with hers. And in the space where a seated man's legs would hang, the sculptor placed the children, a boy and a girl, fingers to their lips, the Egyptian sign for a child. Senetites puts her arm around him. Egyptian texts urged respect for people with disabilities, and two gods, Bes and Ptah, could take the form of dwarfs. Look now at the children, standing exactly where their father's legs would be.

summary: The mother of the Great Pyramid's builder left gold-covered furniture, a sealed stone coffin and no body. Nobody knows where she went.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A bed sloping down to a footboard, a headrest, a carrying chair, armchairs, a curtain box and a tall frame of poles for a bed canopy, all sheathed in gold. Most of the wood is modern: the original had rotted away, and restorers rebuilt it inside the surviving gold and inlay.
story:
On 9 March 1925 a photographer with George Reisner's Harvard and Boston expedition noticed a patch of plaster just east of the Great Pyramid, where he expected bare limestone. Beneath it was a shaft filled with masonry, about 26 metres deep. At the bottom lay a jumble of gold sheet and decayed wood, the remains of royal furniture, and a sealed alabaster sarcophagus. Inscriptions named Hetepheres, a wife of King Sneferu and mother of Khufu.

The team recorded every fragment before lifting it. In 1927 they opened the sarcophagus. It was empty.

Where was the queen? Reisner thought she had first been buried near Sneferu's pyramids at Dahshur, that robbers violated that tomb, and that Khufu had the rest reburied at Giza without knowing the body was gone. Mark Lehner proposed the reverse: this shaft first, a small pyramid nearby second. Others suggest different sequences. Nobody has settled it.

One thing was intact: her alabaster canopic chest. Its four compartments still held organic remains, two in a weak natron solution. It is one of the oldest canopic chests known, and a hint that royal embalming was well under way.
details: The canopy frame: gold-cased poles that held curtains round the bed, a gift from Sneferu according to its inscription.
The carrying chair: gold hieroglyphs on the back give the queen's titles.
The armchairs: one with papyrus flowers, one with the emblem of the goddess Neith.
The headrest at the head of the bed: Egyptians slept on these instead of pillows.
Her silver bracelets with butterflies, if displayed. Silver was rarer than gold in Egypt.
fun_fact: Her bed slopes downhill towards a footboard, and the 'pillow' is a hard headrest. Royal comfort, 4,500 years ago.
narration: If you have found it, this gold-covered furniture belonged to Queen Hetepheres, wife of King Sneferu and mother of Khufu, the builder of the Great Pyramid. In March 1925 a photographer on George Reisner's Harvard and Boston team noticed a patch of plaster beside the Great Pyramid where there should have been bare rock. Under it was a shaft packed with stone, about 26 metres deep. At the bottom lay a heap of gold sheet and crumbling wood: a bed, a canopy, chairs, a curtain box, all collapsed. The team recorded every fragment, and restorers later rebuilt the furniture in new wood inside the original gold. In 1927 they opened her alabaster sarcophagus. It was empty. Reisner thought robbers had wrecked her first tomb at Dahshur, and that Khufu reburied what was left, never told the body was gone. Others reverse the order. Nobody knows. One thing was intact: her canopic chest, still holding her embalmed organs, one of the oldest known. Look now at the bed: it slopes down to the footboard, and the pillow is a hard headrest.

period: Old Kingdom, 3rd Dynasty, reign of Djoser, c. 2650 BC
summary: Carved wooden panels of a 3rd Dynasty official, often billed as the world's first named dentist. The title may really mean 'ivory carver'.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Tall, narrow panels of cedar carved in low relief. Each shows Hesy-Ra standing or seated, holding a staff and sceptre, with a scribe's kit slung over his shoulder: palette, water pot and pen case. Above him, crisp hieroglyphs give his name and titles.
story:
Hesy-Ra served King Djoser, builder of the Step Pyramid, around 2650 BC. His big mud-brick mastaba lies about 260 metres north-east of the pyramid at Saqqara. Mariette found it in 1861, and James Quibell excavated it in 1910-1912. These cedar panels stood in niches along a long corridor, showing him young, middle-aged and old. The corridor walls were painted with patterned mats, furniture and game boards, among the earliest painted tomb decoration known.

One of his titles is often translated 'greatest of the dentists'. The same signs can be read 'greatest of the ivory carvers', so the first-dentist label deserves a raised eyebrow.
details: The scribe's kit on his shoulder: palette, water pot and pen case, the badge of a literate official.
Compare the faces: younger and older versions of the same man across the panels.
The hieroglyphs above him: some of the finest early relief carving anywhere.
fun_fact: His most famous title may be a misreading: 'greatest of the dentists' and 'greatest of the ivory carvers' are written with the same signs.
narration: If you have found them, these carved cedar panels show Hesy-Ra, an official of King Djoser, builder of the Step Pyramid, about 2650 BC. They stood in niches along a corridor of his mud-brick tomb at Saqqara, found by Auguste Mariette in 1861. They show him at different ages, young, middle-aged and old, holding a staff and a sceptre. Over his shoulder hangs his scribe's kit: a palette, a water pot and a pen case. One of his titles is usually translated greatest of the dentists, and it made him famous as the first named dentist in history. But the same signs can mean greatest of the ivory carvers, so be a little sceptical. Look now for the scribe's kit on his shoulder.

summary: The oldest known life-size Egyptian statue: the king of the Step Pyramid, who sat in a sealed room watching the world through two holes.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A seated king in painted limestone, life-size, wrapped in a long close-fitting robe, right arm across his chest, left hand on his thigh. A heavy wig shows under a striped headcloth, and he wears a long beard. The eye sockets are empty: the inlaid eyes were prised out long ago.
story:
The statue was found in 1924-25, during excavations by the Antiquities Service at Saqqara, inside the serdab of the Step Pyramid: a small sealed chamber built against the pyramid's north side. A serdab had no door. Its only openings were two small holes in the front wall, at the height of the statue's eyes, so the king's spirit could look out on the rituals performed there and, many think, at the northern stars that never set. A plaster copy now sits in the serdab in his place.

Djoser ruled around 2650 BC. His official Imhotep is credited with the Step Pyramid, the earliest colossal stone building in Egypt, which began as a square mastaba and grew in stages into a stack of steps.

The robe is probably the one worn for the Sed festival, the jubilee that renewed a king's power, which his pyramid complex celebrates in stone. His feet rest on the Nine Bows, the traditional enemies of Egypt. Even without its eyes, the face is heavy, stern and very human. In his lifetime his monuments called him Netjerikhet; the name Djoser is known from later Egyptian sources.
details: The empty eye sockets: once inlaid, robbed long ago.
The long close-fitting robe, probably the Sed festival garment of royal renewal.
His feet resting on the Nine Bows, the symbolic enemies of Egypt.
The base: look for his Horus name, Netjerikhet, 'divine of body'.
The striped headcloth over a heavy wig, and the long false beard.
fun_fact: Visitors to Saqqara can still peer through the two holes in the serdab and meet the gaze of Djoser's plaster double.
narration: If you have found him, this is King Djoser, from about 2650 BC, and he is the oldest known life-size statue in Egypt. He sat in the dark for more than 4,000 years. His official Imhotep is credited with building him the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first great stone building in Egypt. Against its north side stood a serdab, a tiny sealed room with no door. Its only openings were two small holes in the front wall, at the height of the statue's eyes. Through them the king's spirit could watch the rituals outside and, many think, the northern stars that never set. The Antiquities Service found him there in 1924. A plaster copy now sits in the serdab, still peering through the holes. Look at him. He wears a long, tight robe, probably the cloak of the jubilee festival that renewed a king's power. A heavy wig shows under his striped headcloth, and his feet rest on the nine bows, the symbol of Egypt's enemies. In his own time he was called Netjerikhet. Now look at his eyes. The sockets are empty: robbers dug out the inlays long ago.

summary: Black-skinned, red-crowned and arms crossed like Osiris: the king who reunited Egypt, found because Howard Carter's horse tripped.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A seated king in painted sandstone with jet-black skin, the tall Red Crown of Lower Egypt, a beard and a short white cloak. His arms are crossed over his chest, fists clenched. Heavy legs, big feet, a blunt face: a bold, new style compared with the Old Kingdom.
story:
When Mentuhotep II came to the throne, around 2060 BC, Egypt was split between Thebes in the south and Herakleopolis in the north. He was a Theban, and by about the 39th year of his reign, which lasted 51 years, he had reunited the country and taken a new name, 'He who unites the Two Lands'. Later Egyptians honoured him as a founder of a new age.

His temple at Deir el-Bahari, right beside the temple of Hatshepsut you see on the 21st, was the model for hers. One day Howard Carter, then a young inspector, was riding there when his horse stumbled into a hollow in the forecourt. When he dug it out in 1900, a long tunnel led to a chamber with an empty coffin and this statue, wrapped in linen. The place is still called Bab el-Hosan, the Gate of the Horse.

Why black? Black was the colour of the fertile Nile mud and of Osiris, god of the dead and of rebirth. The crossed arms are Osiris's pose. The white garment is the cloak of the Sed festival, the jubilee that renewed a king's power. Many see the hidden chamber as a symbolic burial: the king as Osiris, waiting to be reborn.
details: The Red Crown of the north, worn by the southern king who conquered it.
Black skin: the colour of Nile mud and of Osiris, god of rebirth, not a portrait of a real complexion.
Arms crossed over the chest: the classic pose of Osiris.
The short white garment: the Sed festival cloak of royal renewal.
The heavy legs and big feet: the bold Theban style of the early Middle Kingdom.
fun_fact: A stumble by Carter's horse named this site, Bab el-Hosan, the Gate of the Horse, more than 20 years before Carter found Tutankhamun.
narration: If you have found him, this black-skinned king with crossed arms is Mentuhotep the Second, and he put Egypt back together. When he came to the throne, around 2060 BC, the country was split between Thebes in the south and rival kings in the north. Mentuhotep, a Theban, reunited it during a reign of 51 years, and later Egyptians remembered him as a founder. His temple at Deir el-Bahari stands right beside Hatshepsut's, which you will see on the 21st, and hers copied his. The way this statue was found is a gift to any guide. One day Howard Carter, then a young inspector, was riding there when his horse stumbled into a hollow. When he dug it out in 1900, a long tunnel led to a chamber holding an empty coffin and this statue, wrapped in linen. The place is still called Bab el Hosan, the Gate of the Horse. Why black skin? Black was the colour of fertile Nile mud and of Osiris, god of rebirth. The crossed arms are Osiris's pose too. Look now at his crown: the Red Crown of the north, worn by a king from the south.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, early reign of Akhenaten, c. 1350 BC
summary: The strangest royal portraits Egypt ever made: a king with a long face, a pot belly and wide hips, carved for a temple to the sun disc.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Huge sandstone figures of the king, arms crossed, holding the crook and flail, many broken off around the knees. The face is long and narrow, with slanting eyes, full lips and a drooping chin; below a pinched waist the belly swells and the hips and thighs spread. Small cartouches are carved on his body like jewellery.
story:
In 1925 workers digging a drainage ditch east of the great temple of Amun at Karnak hit fallen sandstone statues, lying face down and inscribed with the name Amenhotep IV. That was Akhenaten's name in the first years of his reign, before he moved the court to Amarna. Henri Chevrier, chief inspector at Karnak, excavated there on and off for 25 years and found 28 bases. The site belonged to the Gempaaten, 'the Aten is found', a roofless temple to the sun disc whose open court was lined with pillars and colossi.

Nothing in Egyptian art before looks like this. Kings had always been strong, youthful, ideal men. Here the face is stretched, the lips thick, the belly sags, the hips are wide. One colossus seems naked and has no genitals at all.

Why? Doctors have offered diagnoses. Froehlich's syndrome is generally rejected, because sufferers are usually infertile and Akhenaten fathered at least six daughters. Marfan syndrome has never been confirmed. Most Egyptologists prefer a religious reading: the Aten was creator of all life, father and mother at once, and the king, its only son and prophet, took on that double nature. One scholar argued that the naked figure is really Nefertiti in a clinging dress; its feet, which might settle the matter, are lost.

Within a few years the king changed his name and had Amun's name hacked out across Egypt. After his death his temples were torn down in turn.
details: The small cartouches on his chest, arms and belt: the names of the Aten, worn like jewellery.
Crossed arms holding crook and flail, the royal pose of Osiris.
The face in profile: long chin, heavy lips, slanting eyes. Then the swelling belly and wide hips.
The headgear varies between figures. Compare them if more than one is on display.
If the 'naked' colossus is there: no genitals, no kilt. King, queen or god?
fun_fact: When these were carved he was still called Amenhotep, 'Amun is satisfied'. A few years later he was erasing Amun's name from monuments all over Egypt.
narration: If you have found them, these are some of the strangest royal portraits ever made, and they were meant to be. They show Akhenaten early in his reign, around 1350 BC, when he still called himself Amenhotep the Fourth. In 1925 workers digging a drainage ditch just east of Karnak hit huge sandstone statues lying face down. They came from a temple the young king built to the Aten, the sun disc. Look at the face: long and narrow, slanting eyes, thick lips, a hanging chin. Then look down: a narrow waist, a swelling belly, wide hips, heavy thighs. Kings had always been strong, ideal young men. Nothing looked like this. One colossus even seems naked, with no genitals at all. Why? Doctors have proposed diseases, but one is ruled out because he fathered at least six daughters, and Marfan syndrome has never been confirmed. Most Egyptologists prefer a religious reading. The Aten was creator of all life, father and mother of everyone, and the king, its only son, took on that double nature. One scholar argues the naked figure is really Nefertiti in a clinging dress, but the feet that might settle it are lost. Notice the small cartouches carved on his body like jewellery: the names of the Aten. Within a few years he moved to Amarna and had Amun's name hacked out across Egypt. Look now at the belly and hips, and ask: man, woman, or god?

summary: Seven metres of stone in which the queen sits as big as the king: a rare statement about Tiye, a commoner's daughter who became a power in her own right.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A giant limestone group about 7 m high: Amenhotep III and Queen Tiye sit side by side on one throne, the same size, her arm around him. Three small princesses stand in front, the best preserved in the middle. The group is rebuilt from many fragments, and the joins and modern fills show.
story:
Amenhotep III ruled at the height of Egypt's wealth and built on a colossal scale. This group was probably carved around his first jubilee, in the third decade of his reign, and stood on the west bank at Thebes, likely in his vast mortuary temple. It was found in fragments at Medinet Habu in the late 19th century; in 1897 Georges Daressy gathered the pieces, and they were reassembled in Cairo for the opening of the Egyptian Museum in 1902. A rescue excavation on the west bank in 2011 found six more fragments, and the statue is now about 70 percent complete.

The surprise is Tiye. In most royal statues the queen is a small figure by the king's leg. Here she is his equal in size. She was not born royal: her parents were Yuya and Tjuyu, officials from Akhmim. She became one of the most influential women of her time; foreign kings wrote to her directly, and after her husband's death she was consulted about her son, Akhenaten.

The princesses are Henuttaneb in the middle and two partly destroyed sisters, one of them Nebetah. A limestone head of Nebetah from this statue was sold at auction in 2008; a copy is now attached.

The same king's two giant seated statues still guard the site of his temple. The Greeks named them after Memnon, a hero of the Trojan War, and came to hear one 'sing' at dawn. You will see them on the 21st.
details: Tiye's arm around her husband: an equal partner, not an ornament.
The princess in the middle: Henuttaneb, the best preserved of the three daughters.
Scale: the daughters reach only to their parents' knees.
The joins and lighter modern fills between ancient fragments: the statue is about 70 percent original.
Nebetah's head: a copy of the original sold at auction in 2008.
fun_fact: A head of Princess Nebetah from this very statue sold at auction in 2008 for 206,500 dollars. The statue in front of you wears a copy.
narration: If you have found it, you are standing in front of a family portrait 7 metres high. Amenhotep the Third and his great royal wife Tiye sit side by side on one throne, about 1360 BC, when Egypt was at the height of its wealth. Look at the sizes. In most royal statues the queen is a small figure by her husband's leg. Here Tiye is exactly as big as the king, and her arm is around him. That says a lot about her. Tiye was not born royal. Her parents, Yuya and Tjuyu, were officials from Akhmim, and their tomb treasures have their own stop in this guide. She became one of the most powerful women of her age, and foreign kings wrote to her directly. In front stand three of their daughters, tiny, reaching only to their parents' knees. The best preserved, in the middle, is Princess Henuttaneb. The statue stood on the west bank at Thebes, probably in the king's mortuary temple. It was found broken at Medinet Habu, reassembled for the opening of the Egyptian Museum in 1902, and new fragments found in 2011 brought it to about 70 percent complete. The head of another princess, Nebetah, was sold at auction in 2008, so what you see is a copy. On the 21st you will meet this king again: his two giant seated statues, which the Greeks named after Memnon, a hero of Troy. Look now at Tiye's arm around her husband.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, reign of Amenhotep III, c. 1370 BC
summary: Before Tutankhamun, this was the most complete burial ever found in the Valley of the Kings, and its owners were his great-grandparents.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Gilded coffins and masks, chairs, a bed and boxes from tomb KV46, the burial of Yuya and Tjuyu, parents of Queen Tiye. Look for Tjuyu's gilded mask with its calm, smiling face, and the large chair of Princess Sitamun, their granddaughter. The couple's mummies were not among the royal mummies moved to NMEC in 2021; they have been shown at the Tahrir museum.
story:
On 5 February 1905 James Quibell, digging for the American millionaire Theodore Davis, found a stairway in the Valley of the Kings. The tomb had been robbed in antiquity, probably more than once, but it was still crowded: coffins, chests, beds, three chairs, jars and a chariot in nearly perfect condition. Arthur Weigall said it was like entering a town house closed for the summer. When Gaston Maspero arrived to read the names, Davis, in his excitement, nearly touched his candle to a coffin coated in black resin. They went out and came back with electric lights.

The names were Yuya and Tjuyu, parents of Queen Tiye, wife of Amenhotep III. Yuya was Master of the Horse, a priest of Min at Akhmim and 'god's father', probably as the king's father-in-law. Some Egyptologists think he was of foreign, perhaps Syrian, origin; nothing in the tomb proves it. If the 2010 DNA study is right that both of Tutankhamun's parents were children of Amenhotep III and Tiye, the couple were his great-grandparents twice over.

Their mummies are among the best preserved from Egypt. Yuya still has white wavy hair; CT scans suggest both died aged about 50 to 60.
details: Tjuyu's gilded mask: the gentle face and black-rimmed eyes.
Sitamun's chair: the large chair of the couple's granddaughter, a daughter of Amenhotep III.
The jewellery box with Amenhotep III's cartouche: its jewels were taken by ancient thieves.
The nested coffins, gilded and silvered, one inside the other.
Yuya's chariot, if displayed: one of the few complete chariots to survive from ancient Egypt.
fun_fact: Davis almost set the tomb alight: in his excitement he held his candle close to a coffin covered in flammable black resin.
narration: If you have found them, these gilded masks, coffins and chairs belonged to Yuya and Tjuyu, the parents of Queen Tiye, and so Tutankhamun's great-grandparents. If the DNA study is right, twice over, because both his parents were children of Tiye. In February 1905 James Quibell, digging for the American millionaire Theodore Davis, found their tomb in the Valley of the Kings, K V 46. It had been robbed in antiquity, but the room was still crowded with coffins, chests, beds, chairs and even a chariot. One of the excavators said it was like entering a town house shut up for the summer. When the great Egyptologist Gaston Maspero came to read the names, Davis, in his excitement, nearly held his candle against a coffin coated in black resin. They came back with electric lights. Yuya was Master of the Horse and a priest of Min at Akhmim. Some think he came from abroad, perhaps from Syria, but nothing proves it. Look now for Tjuyu's gilded mask, and its gentle smile.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, year 5 of Merneptah, c. 1208 BC
summary: A victory hymn in black granite with one line that made it famous: the oldest known mention of Israel outside the Bible.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A round-topped slab of black granite over 3 m high, covered in 28 lines of hieroglyphs. At the top, the king appears before the gods of Thebes. The famous name is near the bottom, in line 27.
story:
Merneptah, the 13th son of Ramesses II, came to the throne already old. In his 5th year, about 1208 BC, he defeated a Libyan invasion helped by Sea Peoples allies, and had a victory hymn carved. His masons did not even cut a new stone: they used the rough back of a stele of Amenhotep III.

Flinders Petrie found it in 1896 in Merneptah's funerary temple at Thebes, and Wilhelm Spiegelberg translated it. Most of the text celebrates the Libyan war. Near the end comes Canaan: Ashkelon, Gezer and Yanoam are taken, and then 'Israel is laid waste, its seed is no more.' Petrie predicted the stele would be better known than anything else he had found. He was right.

The detail scholars argue over is a single sign. The towns carry the determinative for a city or land. Israel carries the sign for a people, a seated man and woman. Most read it as a group living in Canaan around 1200 BC, not yet a kingdom. A few prefer other readings, such as 'Jezreel', but most Egyptologists accept Israel.
details: Line 27, near the bottom: the name Israel, followed by the seated man and woman meaning 'people'.
The other Canaanite names nearby: Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam, each with the sign for a place.
The rounded top: the king before the gods of Thebes.
If you can see the back: the older text of Amenhotep III, whose stele was reused.
fun_fact: The oldest known mention of Israel outside the Bible is written on the back of somebody else's monument.
narration: If you have found it, this tall black granite slab carries the oldest known mention of Israel outside the Bible. Merneptah, the thirteenth son of Ramesses the Second, came to the throne already old. In his fifth year, about 1208 BC, he beat back an invasion of Libyans and their allies from the Sea Peoples, and had a victory hymn carved. His masons did not even cut a new stone. They used the back of a stele of Amenhotep the Third. Flinders Petrie found it in 1896 in Merneptah's temple at Thebes. Most of the 28 lines celebrate the Libyan war. But near the end comes a list of beaten places in Canaan: Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam, and then: Israel is laid waste, its seed is no more. The towns carry the sign for a city or a land. Israel carries the sign for a people, a seated man and woman. Most scholars take this as a people living in Canaan around 1200 BC, not yet a kingdom. Petrie said this stele would be better known than anything else he found. He was right. Look now near the bottom, in the second-last line.

period: Third Intermediate Period, 21st Dynasty, c. 1000 BC
summary: A gold mask and a solid silver coffin from the only Egyptian royal tomb found fully intact, discovered in 1940 just as the world looked away.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. The gold mask, about 48 cm high, with lapis lazuli and eyes and brows inlaid in black and white glass. Nearby, if shown together, are the king's silver coffin inlaid with gold, gold sheaths for his fingers and toes, and gold sandals. It was made about 300 years after Tutankhamun's mask.
story:
By the 21st Dynasty Egypt was divided: priest-generals held Thebes in the south while kings ruled the north from Tanis, in the eastern Delta. Psusennes I reigned there for several decades around 1000 BC.

In 1939 the French archaeologist Pierre Montet found royal tombs inside the temple enclosure at Tanis. In one chamber lay a silver coffin with a falcon's head, made for King Sheshonq II, reburied there after his own tomb flooded. In February 1940 Montet reached the sealed burial chamber of Psusennes himself: the only Egyptian royal tomb found fully intact. The pharaoh Amenemope and the general Wendjebauendjed were buried in the same tomb.

The news barely travelled. In May 1940 Germany invaded France, and the gold of Tanis spent the war in obscurity. It is still far less famous than Tutankhamun's.

Psusennes lay in a nest of coffins. The outer sarcophagus had first been made for Merneptah, son of Ramesses II, and was reused. Inside, the innermost coffin was silver inlaid with gold, and in Egypt silver was considerably rarer than gold. The Delta's damp destroyed the wood and most of the body. In 1940 the anatomist Douglas Derry found an old man with worn teeth, an abscess and arthritis that probably crippled him at the end.
details: The mask's eyes and brows: inlaid black and white glass.
The silver coffin: silver had to be imported, and in Egypt it was rarer than gold.
Gold sheaths for fingers and toes, and gold sandals, to keep the body whole forever.
Sheshonq II's silver coffin with a falcon's head, if displayed nearby.
Compare with Tutankhamun's mask, about 300 years older: the same idea, a different face.
fun_fact: Tanis is the 'lost city' where Indiana Jones digs up the Ark in Raiders of the Lost Ark. The real Tanis gold is better, and real.
narration: If you have found it, this is the other gold mask of Egypt. It belonged to Psusennes the First, who ruled from the city of Tanis in the Nile Delta around 1000 BC, three centuries after Tutankhamun. In 1939 the French archaeologist Pierre Montet was digging inside the temple enclosure at Tanis when he found royal tombs. In one chamber lay a silver coffin with a falcon's head, made for King Sheshonq the Second. In February 1940 he reached the sealed burial of Psusennes himself, untouched by robbers: the only royal tomb in Egypt found fully intact. And almost nobody noticed. In May Germany invaded France, and the gold of Tanis spent the war in obscurity. Even now it is far less famous than Tutankhamun's. The king lay in a stone sarcophagus first made for Merneptah, son of Ramesses the Second, and reused. Inside was a coffin of silver, inlaid with gold, and in Egypt silver was rarer than gold. On the mummy lay this mask, gold with lapis lazuli, the eyes and brows in black and white glass. The damp of the Delta destroyed the wood and most of the body. What remained showed an old man with bad teeth and arthritis. If the name Tanis sounds familiar, it is the lost city in the first Indiana Jones film. Look now at the mask's eyes, and compare them in your mind with Tutankhamun's.

period: Late 17th to early 18th Dynasty, c. 1550 BC
summary: Three golden flies for bravery and an axe showing King Ahmose smiting an enemy, buried with a queen of the war against the Hyksos.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Look for three large gold flies on a chain, stylised and almost modern, and a ceremonial axe whose blade shows the king smiting an enemy, with a griffin. Nearby may be little model boats in gold and silver from the same burial.
story:
In 1859 workmen of Auguste Mariette found a queen's coffin at Dra Abu el-Naga in Thebes. The body was destroyed soon afterwards, but the treasure survived: objects naming King Ahmose, who drove the Hyksos out and began the New Kingdom, and King Kamose, who fought them before him. The coffin named a queen Ahhotep.

For a century she was taken to be Ahhotep I, mother of Ahmose, praised on a Karnak stela for looking after Egypt and holding its soldiers together. Many scholars now think she was a second Ahhotep, possibly Kamose's wife. The golden flies were an award for valour, and the axe's griffin is in Aegean style, a hint of contacts with Minoan Crete.
details: The three golden flies: big stylised wings and eyes, hung on a gold chain. A military decoration.
The axe blade: Ahmose smiting a kneeling enemy, and a griffin in Aegean style.
Gold and silver model boats with tiny rowers, if displayed.
fun_fact: Egyptian soldiers won flies, not medals, perhaps because a fly keeps coming back however often you swat it.
narration: If you have found them, these three golden flies are an ancient medal for bravery. They come from the coffin of a queen named Ahhotep, found in 1859 at Dra Abu el Naga in Thebes by workmen of Auguste Mariette. She was buried with weapons and jewels naming King Ahmose, who drove the Hyksos out of Egypt, and King Kamose, who fought them before him. For a century people assumed she was Ahmose's mother, praised on a stela at Karnak for caring for Egypt in wartime. Many scholars now think she was a second Ahhotep, perhaps Kamose's wife. Why flies? Perhaps because a fly keeps coming back, however often you swat it. Look for the axe too: Ahmose smiting an enemy, and a griffin in Minoan style.
